## Week 1, Session 2 — Simple linear regression {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression}

<div class="callout callout-note">
**Inference labs** use the five-step template:
Hypothesis → Visualise → Assumptions → Conduct → Conclude.
</div>

### Learning objectives {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-learning-objectives}

- Fit a simple linear regression with `lm()` and read the output.
- Produce a tidy coefficient table with intervals using `broom`.
- Draw the fitted line on the scatterplot and express the slope in the
  units of the variables.

### Prerequisites {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-prerequisites}

Correlation vs regression; basic comfort with ggplot2.

### Background {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-background}

Simple linear regression models the mean of a response Y as a linear
function of a single predictor X. The model is Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε with
the error term ε assumed independent, zero-mean, and of constant
variance. The slope β₁ is the expected change in Y for a one-unit
change in X; the intercept β₀ is the expected Y at X = 0, which is
sometimes meaningful and sometimes only a device for anchoring the
line.

Although the formulas are old, the habits they require are modern:
always plot first, always report an interval, and always read the slope
back in the units of the variables. A regression coefficient is only
useful if the reader can imagine the units on the axis.

The default `summary()` printout from `lm()` is dense. A clean way to
read a fit is to use `broom::tidy()` for coefficients and
`broom::glance()` for global quantities such as R² and residual
standard error, and then plot the line on the data to sanity-check.

### Setup {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-setup}

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(palmerpenguins)
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

### 1. Hypothesis {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-1-hypothesis}

Among Adelie penguins, does bill length predict body mass?

Null: slope of body mass on bill length is zero.
Alternative: slope is non-zero.

### 2. Visualise {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-2-visualise}

```r
ad <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie") |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)

ggplot(ad, aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)")
```

The cloud climbs gently from left to right. The smoothed line is an
honest guess at the conditional mean.

### 3. Assumptions {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-3-assumptions}

Linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, and approximate normality of
residuals.

```r
fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm, data = ad)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Residuals vs fitted is patternless; QQ is close to straight. No single
point dominates.

### 4. Conduct {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-4-conduct}

```r
tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
glance(fit) |> select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, p.value)
```

```r
slope <- coef(fit)[2]
ci <- confint(fit)[2, ]
```

### 5. Concluding statement {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-5-concluding-statement}

> Among Adelie penguins (*n* = `nrow(ad)`), each additional mm of
> bill length was associated with an increase of
> `round(slope, 0)` g in body mass (95% CI:
> `round(ci[1], 0)` to `round(ci[2], 0)` g;
> *p* = `signif(glance(fit)$p.value, 2)`). Bill length explained
> `round(100 * glance(fit)$r.squared, 1)`% of the variance in body
> mass.


### Common pitfalls {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-simple-linear-regression-common-pitfalls}

- Extrapolating beyond the range of X.
- Interpreting the intercept when X = 0 is nonsensical.
- Quoting R² without reporting the slope and its interval.
